tensions.name: Horizon: fixed investor trait or movable behaviour

side_a.position: Trading horizon is a persistent investor characteristic; investors specialise by frequency
side_a.evidence: Investor fixed effect in trading frequency (Parsa); endogenous frequency specialisation and persistent fund turnover (Crouzet et al.); holding-horizon deciles persist for 20 quarters (Lan-Moneta-Wermers)

side_b.evidence: Average fund turnover swings 59%-102% a year with a strong common component (Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor); evolving horizon mix in ABMs (LeBaron)

tensions.resolution: Both hold at different levels: ranks persist while levels move. For peer-effect purposes what matters is the idiosyncratic within-institution residual after quarter (and style-quarter) effects; project data show 33% of variance left after institution and quarter FE, so the trait view does not kill Pivot A, but the paper must report this decomposition first.

tensions.name: Peer influence versus correlated effects in institutional turnover

side_a.evidence: Intransitive triads identify endogenous effects (Bramoulle-Djebbari-Fortin); peers' idiosyncratic shocks as instruments (Leary-Roberts; Georg-Pierret-Steffen)

side_b.position: Correlated effects and sampling defeat observational network designs
side_b.evidence: Common turnover component (Pastor-Stambaugh-Taylor); same-horizon flow comovement 0.80 vs 0.12 (Chan-Cheng-Hameed); FoF IV invalid in sampled networks (Chandrasekhar-Lewis); weak in dense networks (Canen-Chadha); outcome-on-mean regressions vacuous (Angrist)

tensions.resolution: Side B wins for the design as currently specified. A credible Pivot A needs exogenous shocks to neighbours (filer mergers/closures, manager departures) on a full-universe network with style x quarter FE; FoF IV only as robustness with Anderson-Rubin sets.

tensions.name: Does horizon diversity stabilise or destabilise prices

side_a.position: Diversity stabilises: more liquidity, lower volatility
side_a.evidence: Higher holder churn dispersion -> lower illiquidity and lower return volatility, with a 2003 tax-reform shock (Chan-Cheng-Hameed incl. IA1); FMH ABMs (Li-Nishimura-Men; Li-Li-Sun); CME stock-level slope

side_b.evidence: Mixed-horizon populations raise variability (LeBaron); heterogeneity raises volatility on overlap networks (Forera et al.); CME's simulated friction channel

tensions.resolution: Side A has the stronger evidence (empirical, quasi-experimental). The CME friction channel is the outlier and should be withdrawn or replaced by a calibrated liquidity channel.

tensions.name: Who absorbs short-horizon selling in a crash

side_a.evidence: Outside liquidity from long-run investors (Bolton-Santos-Scheinkman); long-term IO mitigated COVID losses (level); insurers/pensions countercyclical (Timmer)

side_b.position: Retail and arbitrageurs absorb; institutions co-trade
side_b.evidence: Retail bought while institutions sold in 2020Q1 (Glossner et al.); long-horizon holders also sold, 7% vs 21% (Cella et al.); same-direction trading by other managers (Barbon et al.)

tensions.resolution: Side B on absolute absorption; the defensible claim is relative (long-horizon holders sell less), testable within stock with a Coval-Stafford flow-induced instrument. Worth a section, not a paper.

tensions.name: Is horizon homophily in co-holding a fact or an artefact

side_a.evidence: CME kappa-hat 0.158 positive in all quarters; type-assortative cliques (Crane-Koch-Michaely); excess validated overlap links (Gualdi et al.)

side_b.position: Mechanical from indexing, drift-contaminated tau and characteristic demand
side_b.evidence: Characteristic-based demand (Koijen-Yogo); shared asset managers (Ozdagli-Ryfe); price-drift contamination of value-weight tau

tensions.resolution: Side B for the raw measure. Only an active-weight, share-based, dyadic-FE, BiCM-validated residual would be a fact, and it is a motivating fact for A, not a contribution.

tensions.name: Short-horizon institutions: destabilising or informed

side_a.evidence: Short-term IO drives crash risk (Zhu); high-turnover large institutions raise volatility (Ben-David et al.); short-horizon sell more in turmoil (Cella et al.)

side_b.evidence: Short-term institutions' trades forecast returns (Yan-Zhang); benefits of short-horizon investors (Giannetti-Yu)

tensions.resolution: Scoped differently (stability vs information); both right. The pivot should not frame short-horizon investors as simply bad: horizon contagion matters because it changes the mix, not because short horizons are harmful per se.
